A sheep-bone flute from West Yorkshire was dated to the Iron Age in 1952, and later research holds it to be post-Roman; the Bute Island museum has a flute that is securely Iron Age. The Wicklow pipe may be the oldest duct instrument; the original is incomplete, and a copy fitted with a duct can be played. Early Irish law mentions feadan players, and the oldest surviving whistle dates from the twelfth century. Six-hole whistles of brass or bronze from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and recorders from Dordrecht, Göttingen and elsewhere, show that the instrument developed in many parts of Europe.

Opening and closing the fingerholes changes the length of the vibrating air column, which shifts the pitch. Compared with the transverse flute, the duct structure is more fixed, so the player has less freedom to adjust volume and intonation directly and has to rely on other structural details to compensate.
